## Upper Bound

Suppose we have k valid triples. Since a_i + b_i + c_i = n for each i, summing over all i:

$$kn = \sum a_i + \sum b_i + \sum c_i$$

Each of {a_i}, {b_i}, {c_i} is a set of k distinct non-negative integers (each ≤ n). The minimum possible sum of k distinct non-negative integers is 0 + 1 + ⋯ + (k−1) = k(k−1)/2. Therefore:

$$kn \geq 3 \cdot \frac{k(k-1)}{2} \implies n \geq \frac{3(k-1)}{2} \implies k \leq \frac{2n}{3} + 1$$

Since k is an integer: **k ≤ ⌊2n/3⌋ + 1**.

Write n = 3q + r, r ∈ {0,1,2}. The bound gives:

| r | N(n) = ⌊2n/3⌋+1 |

| 0 | 2q + 1 |
| 1 | 2q + 1 |
| 2 | 2q + 2 |

**Case n = 3q (k = 2q+1):** Set a_i = i for i = 0,…,2q. Define:

- Even i = 2j (j = 0,…,q): b_i = 2q − j, giving sums i + b_i = 2q + j ∈ {2q,…,3q}
- Odd i = 2j+1 (j = 0,…,q−1): b_i = q−1−j, giving sums i + b_i = q + j ∈ {q,…,2q−1}

Then c_i = 3q − i − b_i. The b-values are {0,…,2q} (permutation ✓), the sums {i+b_i} = {q,…,3q} are all distinct, so c-values = {0,…,2q} (permutation ✓). All sums equal 3q ✓.

**Case n = 3q+2 (k = 2q+2):** Set a_i = i for i = 0,…,2q+1. Define:

- Even i = 2j (j = 0,…,q): b_i = 2q+2−j, sums = 2q+2+j ∈ {2q+2,…,3q+2}
- Odd i = 2j+1 (j = 0,…,q): b_i = q−j, sums = q+1+j ∈ {q+1,…,2q+1}
